title: Prophecy, Not Blasphemy
english: …who works mighty deeds that we cannot bear; over whom we have wasted away with jealousy and envy; whom the deaf man obeys when he is called; to whom the blind man looks and sees, having received his eyes from him; from whose tongue the lame man asks for feet, and borrows hands as well; through whom the beds of the sick have been emptied; through whom there is no difference between the healthy and the sick; through whom lepers have forgotten their disease; through whom there is no need of physicians; through whom the medicines people grind are useless.”

“This man does not stop speaking words against this holy place and the law” (Acts 6:13). What words are these? “For we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses handed down to us” (Acts 6:14). Rightly are you called false witnesses and slanderers, because you speak the truth as though it were not the truth; because you call blasphemies against God the prophecies that came from him and concern this place; and because you count as a setting aside of the law the very things he himself threatened would come to pass.

For whose voice is this, whose prophecy, whose proclamation? Who commanded Isaiah, who commanded Micah to speak in this way: “Therefore because of you Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall be like a hut for watching fruit” (Micah 3:12); “The daughter of Zion shall be left like a booth in a vineyard and like a hut in a cucumber field” (Isaiah 1:8)? Who inspired David as well to say such things: “Remember, Lord, against the sons of Edom the day of Jerusalem, those who said, ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundation’” (Psalm 137:7)?

And what of Moses? Does he not also cast his vote with what Stephen said? Did he not write down these curses of yours, which have now come true in plain experience and which let everyone see the causes for which they were pronounced? Let the wounds that befell the Jewish people be set beside the words of Moses. If you examine them word for word, you will find that they came to pass without being false anywhere in anything, small or great. “And if after this you walk crookedly” (Leviticus 26:21): for they never kept their heart straight toward God, and far less in the later times, when they swerved from the call of Christ. Therefore he went on: “And if you will not obey me” – and indeed they did not obey when Christ called – “I will bring seven more plagues on you according to your lawless deeds” (Leviticus 26:21). For since they denied the seven gifts of the Spirit, the seven spirits of wickedness, which entered and dwelt in them, become seven plagues for them; and their last state became worse than the first (Matthew 12:45).

“And I will send against you the wild beasts of the earth” (Leviticus 26:22). He means the nations; for formerly, through their ignorance, they were beasts, because they worshiped the divine in the image of beasts and four-footed creatures and reptiles (Romans 1:23). Cursing them, David said: “May those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8). These are the nations God has now sent against them, and they do what the lawgiver says next: “And they shall devour you, and consume your cattle, and make you few; and your roads shall be deserted” (Leviticus 26:22). For every one of these things has happened to them, both visibly and spiritually, since they have been ruled by the nations.

Yet God did not stop the threats he spoke through Moses to the thankless people at this point, but set out others harsher and greater than these. For he says: “You shall take a wife, and another man shall have her. You shall build a house, and you shall not live in it. You shall plant a vineyard, and you shall not gather its grapes. Your calf shall be slaughtered before you, and you shall not eat of it” (Deuteronomy 28:30-31). And after threatening many other things besides these, he did not hide the cause from which these things come, but brings it in with a host of threats that are joined to the ones we have just quoted: “And your life shall hang before your eyes; and you shall fear day and night, and you shall not believe in your life. In the morning you shall say, ‘When will it be evening?’ And in the evening you shall say, ‘When will it be morning?’ because of the fear of your heart, with which you shall fear, and because of the sights of your eyes, which you shall see” (Deuteronomy 28:66-67).

Hear, then, how these things end; hear also how they come to pass, and do not blame Stephen for addressing the people in agreement with the law and the prophets. “You shall take a wife”: the old covenant; “and another man shall have her”: for the people from the nations has gained it. “You shall build a house, and you shall not live in it”: the temple, plainly, for you see it fallen. “You shall plant a vineyard, and you shall not gather its grapes”: for it bore not grapes but thorns (Isaiah 5:2). Or let us also take the vineyard to mean the vine that is Christ…
translator_notes: The section opens mid-sentence inside the accusers' description of Stephen, begun in the previous section, and ends mid-sentence.
Leviticus 26:21 follows the Greek (LXX) wording, 'walk crookedly' (πλάγιοι); Hesychius takes up the word with ἐπλαγίαζον, 'they swerved' from the call of Christ.
Psalm 137:7 is LXX Psalm 136:7, and Psalm 115:8 is LXX Psalm 113:16.
'You shall not believe in your life' (Deuteronomy 28:66) is kept close to the Greek (οὐ πιστεύσεις), because the next section argues that unbelief is the cause of fear.

title: The Day That Was Neither Day nor Night
english: …for Christ came from them (Romans 9:5), the vine of our life (John 15:1); but it is we who gather his grapes, we who mix the wine, we who drink the new wine. “Your calf shall be slaughtered before you, and you shall not eat of it”: for theirs is the sacrifice of Christ – they led the calf from heaven up to the altar – but ours is the supper, ours the table.

And for what reason? Because they fell sick with unbelief, brought ignorance instead of knowledge, and at the time for theology slid into blasphemy. They entered the bridal chamber and did not receive the Bridegroom; they wreathed the wedding hall and refused the marriage; and when the cross was carried out, the elements were shaken, but they were not changed. For this is what he added next: “And your life shall hang before your eyes” (Deuteronomy 28:66). What is the life? Christ, who says: “I am the way and the life and the truth” (John 14:6). And where does it hang? On the wood of the cross. For he who hung the earth by a word (Job 26:7) hangs on the wood; on it he who carries is carried, he who suspends is suspended, he who lifts up is lifted up: “For when I am lifted up,” he says, “I will draw all to myself” (John 12:32). “And you shall fear day and night, and you shall not believe in your life” (Deuteronomy 28:66). So unbelief has become the cause of fear.

“You shall fear day and night”: for day and night were the same, because “there was darkness over all the land from the sixth hour” (Matthew 27:45). Hence Zechariah is at a loss what he ought rather to name it, what it is fitting to call it: whether the time of the cross should take its name from the darkness that fell or from the daylight that by rule belonged to it. So he says: “And on that day there shall be no light; and there shall be cold and frost. It is a great day; it shall be known to the Lord; not day nor night; and toward evening there shall be light. And on that day living water shall go out from Jerusalem, half of it to the first sea and half of it to the last sea” (Zechariah 14:6-8). These things happened both visibly and spiritually.

“On that day there shall be no light”: for the sun set at midday, and darkness and ignorance had been poured over the hearts of the Jews. “There shall be cold and frost.” Peter bears witness to this, warming himself by the charcoal fire because the winter season was at its height (John 18:18). But beyond this there was cold and frost, because the love of the Jews toward God had then grown especially cold; for otherwise they would not have crucified the Savior and Redeemer who came from him. “It is a great day.” How could it not be great, the day on which Adam was formed anew, sin was abolished, death was destroyed, the potter received back his vessel, the shepherd his sheep, the merchant his pearl? “It shall be known to God.” For how could he who knows all things not recognize above all that day, on which he gave up his only-begotten Son for sacrifice? “Not day nor night”: since by its course it was day, not night. “Toward evening there shall be light”: when, after the ninth hour, the darkness ceased. So the same time was both night and day.

“And living water shall go out from Jerusalem.” From where? From the side of the Life (John 19:34); for from the place where Eve was formed, from there the Church is fittingly formed (Genesis 2:21-22). “Half of it into the first sea”: that is, the sea of baptism. “And half of it into the last sea”: plainly, the sea of repentance. For the tears of repentance are what remains of the gift of baptism, and the proof is clear: one who has not been baptized repents in vain unless he hastens to be baptized; in vain he offers his prayer as a sacrifice, in vain he asks for pardon, in vain he pours out a spring of tears. For without baptism forgiveness of sins does not take place. But one who has been baptized has a repentance that works: he weeps and is set free; he groans and mourns and prays, and at once he is cleansed.

But hear also how the rest of the law’s prediction comes to pass: “In the morning you shall say, ‘When will it be evening?’ And in the evening you shall say, ‘When will it be morning?’” From what cause? “From the fear of your heart, with which you shall fear, and from the sights of your eyes, which you shall see” (Deuteronomy 28:67). Because of the signs and wonders that were being done at the time of the cross – the earth quaking, the sun fleeing, the sky hiding, the rocks splitting, the veil tearing, the tombs opening (Matthew 27:51-52) – they were afraid and troubled, and so they were naturally driven to say to one another: “When will it be evening, so that we may take the Life down from the cross, hide in the earth the one who came from heaven,…
translator_notes: The section opens mid-sentence; the words of the Jews at its end continue into the next section.
John 14:6 is quoted in Hesychius's order: 'the way and the life and the truth'.
Zechariah 14:6-8 follows the Greek (LXX) wording. Hesychius quotes 'known to the Lord' and then comments on 'known to God'; both are kept as he wrote them.

title: The Heavens Opened
english: …shut up the Immortal in a tomb, and rid ourselves of the wonder from which such great terrors come upon us?”

But even when they had done these things, they gained nothing of their aim; what they attempted turned out the opposite for them. And this is why in the evening they said, “When will it be morning?” For again the wonders worked in the night of the resurrection were fearful: they saw the tomb as a bridal chamber, the grave sealed and the dead man running out alive, the soldiers like dead men (Matthew 28:4), the women bearing myrrh, angels guarding the linen cloths, and another sitting on the stone as herald of the resurrection (Matthew 28:2). Then they said: “When will it be morning, so that we may give silver to the soldiers, so that we may corrupt Pilate, so that we may steal the truth by deceit, so that we may spread the report ‘that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep’?” (Matthew 28:12-14).

This is the testimony the law bears, and Moses through it, or rather God in each of them, against the thankless people; and Stephen the theologian, for convicting that people, is called a blasphemer by them. And the high priest says: “Are these things so?” (Acts 7:1). Do you not know how they are? Did you not contrive the plot? Did you not hire the slanderers? Are not the witnesses of the deceit in your pay? “But there is need,” he says, “of falsehood and pretense, and we need deceit for the trap we have laid. So we sold Joseph (Genesis 37:28), so we murdered Naboth (1 Kings 21:13), so we crucified Christ.”

But Stephen, having found an occasion for teaching, poured many saving words into the people’s ears, and as the conclusion of his speech he brought in words fit for him to say, as a witness of the truth, and for them to hear, as men bent on fighting against God and sick with opposition to the Spirit: “Hard-hearted and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you” (Acts 7:51).

And how is it that at the beginning you say, “Men, brothers and fathers, hear me” (Acts 7:2)? “Those words,” he says, “belong to the nobility of Abraham, these to the wickedness of these men. Those belong to the good root, these to the bad branches. Those show what is distinguished in the flock, these the unruliness, the hardness, the unbridled temper of the many.” Isaiah urged him toward that opening: “Say ‘Our brothers’ to those who hate us and abhor us, so that the name of the Lord may be glorified” (Isaiah 66:5). But toward this ending they themselves forced his speech, even against his will: “I called them brothers, I addressed them as fathers, so that no one would think I was accusing them as enemies or refuting them as foes. But I called the same men hard-hearted and uncircumcised, since truth must be put before kinship, and one must not spare friends or brothers or fathers or any other relatives when they break the law.”

Yet the children of the Jews could not bear these words, but gnashed their teeth like wild beasts, eager to swallow Stephen up while he was still speaking. “They gnashed their teeth” (Acts 7:54). For of them it had been said: “Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Psalm 57:4). But Stephen kept his eyes not on them but on God, and leaving the earth behind he hastened toward the courts of heaven, and with a ringing voice he proclaimed: “Look, I see the heavens opened” (Acts 7:56). That is: the gain is shared, the way is ready for all, the gate has been opened to those who wish to enter. Let the brave man contend with all his strength; let the true soldier now use his weapons, now show the greatness of his might. For the one who presides over the contest is watching; he stands ready, handing out the crowns and the prizes.

“Look, I see the heavens opened.” And he did not leave the one who wishes to know in ignorance of who opened them. For this reason he cried out: “and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:56), meaning God the Word made flesh. For since the Son of God has become Son of Man, since he who is from the Father has himself come from a virgin and stood as the common border of earth and the heavens, the dividing wall of enmity has been taken away (Ephesians 2:14), the barrier is out of the way, and citizenship is shared by angels and men, if men are willing. Those who are on earth may serve as soldiers in heaven, be below in the flesh and present above in the spirit, be with the clay by the clay, but with God by the mind.
Such, then, was the theology Stephen proclaimed; but disorderly shouts followed his orderly theology, and shout followed shout; and stones from slings followed the teachings of the holy laws.
translator_notes: The section opens mid-sentence, closing the words of the Jews begun in the previous section.
τοὺς στρατιώτας <ὡς> νεκρούς: the editor's supplement 'like' is followed, so 'the soldiers like dead men' (Matthew 28:4).
Acts 7:51: Hesychius reads σκληροκάρδιοι, 'hard-hearted', where the usual text of Acts has σκληροτράχηλοι, 'stiff-necked'; the English follows Hesychius.
The last sentence ('and stones from slings followed the teachings of the holy laws') runs across into the next section in the Greek; it is translated whole here.
